subject: Groundwater under Delhi and across India — the other water, and the one nobody sees
transcription: Read off the source PDF, once, and COMMITTED. Every figure is quoted with the table it came from. The category counts were checked against their own row totals before being written down.

source.name: Central Ground Water Board, Department of Water Resources, RD & GR, Ministry of Jal Shakti
source.publication: National Compilation on Dynamic Ground Water Resources of India, 2025
source.why_this_document: A page about a dead river is only half the water story. When the surface water fails, a city goes underground — and this is the official annual account of what is left down there. It is the same ministry that answers for the Yamuna.

kind_note: Recharge and extraction are ESTIMATED by a published methodology, not metered. CGWB itself calls them assessments. They are the official figures and they are the best that exist; they are not meter readings.

method.unit: an assessment unit is a block, mandal or taluk
method.stage_of_extraction: annual groundwater extraction divided by annual extractable groundwater resource, as a percentage
method.categories: Safe, Semi-Critical, Critical, Over-Exploited — assigned from that ratio
method.plain: Stage of extraction is how much of the water that refills each year is taken out each year. Under 70 per cent is Safe. Above 100 per cent means the aquifer is being spent, not used — the balance comes out of storage that does not come back.

national.share_not_safe_note: the report's own wording: 'around 25% have been categorized as Overexploited, Critical, or Semi-Critical'
national.quote: In the present assessment (for the assessment year 2025), the total annual groundwater recharge and annual extractable groundwater resources in the country have been assessed at 448.68 bcm and 407.88 bcm, respectively. The annual groundwater extraction has been estimated at 247.18 bcm, with the average stage of groundwater extraction in the country at 60.6%.

checks.note: The four category counts sum to the stated total of 34 and the percentages to 100. Checked before transcription.

not_safe_units.reading: Twenty-seven of Delhi's thirty-four assessment units are Semi-Critical, Critical or Over-Exploited. Seven are Safe.

critical_or_worse.reading: Twenty-one of thirty-four are Critical or Over-Exploited.

the_reading.headline: Delhi takes out 92 of every 100 litres its aquifers put back.
the_reading.why_it_belongs_on_a_river_page: The Yamuna enters Delhi fit to drink at Palla and leaves it with no measurable oxygen. When surface water fails, a city goes underground — and Delhi's underground is at 92.1 per cent, with 21 of its 34 assessment units Critical or Over-Exploited. There is no spare water source. That is the sentence the two documents make together, and neither says it alone.
the_reading.the_honest_limit: This is a correlation of two official assessments, not a causal claim. Delhi's groundwater is drawn down for many reasons, and this page does not assert that river pollution is one of them. What it asserts is only that both of the city's water sources are in the state their own regulators describe.

holes: There is no public per-borewell or per-ward groundwater level feed. The assessment is annual and by block.

Groundwater QUALITY in Delhi — salinity, nitrate, fluoride — is assessed in separate CGWB reports that were not parsed for this build. Quantity and quality are different measurements and only quantity is published here.
Nothing here links a specific groundwater figure to a specific river reading. No such published analysis was found.
Recharge and extraction are modelled estimates by a published method, not metered volumes.
caveats: Stage of extraction above 100 per cent means storage is being spent. Below it does not mean the water is safe to drink — that is a quality question this table does not answer.
A block is a large area. A Safe block can contain a failing neighbourhood.
The figures are the assessment year's, not today's.
Comparing states by stage of extraction compares ratios, not volumes. Punjab at 156 per cent and Delhi at 92 are different sizes of problem in the same units.
